'''Jacqueline M. Grebmeier''' is an American ecologist who specializes in polar biological oceanography.

==Early life and education==
Grebmeier completed her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in Zoology from the [[University of California, Davis]] in 1977 before enrolling at [[Stanford University]] for her first [[Master's degree]] in Biology. Following this, she earned her second master's degree in Marine Affairs from the [[University of Washington]] in 1983,<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=The role of science in the Alaskan Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas leasing decision process|date=1983|language=English|first=Jacqueline Mary|last=Grebmeier|oclc = 10168522}}</ref> specializing in applications of Arctic science to Arctic resource utilization policy, and her PhD in Biological Oceanography from the [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]] in 1987.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Jacqueline M. Grebmeier |url=https://mypages.unh.edu/arctic-change/jackie-grebmeier |publisher=University of New Hampshire |access-date=June 6, 2021}}</ref>

==Career==
Upon completing her PhD, Grebmeier joined the faculty at the [[University of Tennessee]] in 1989. As a research [[associate professor]] of ecology and evolutionary biology, she was the project co-leader on a joint U.S.-Russian study of ecosystems in the Bering and Chukchi seas and an advisor to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[National Science Foundation]]. In 2000, Grebmeier was selected by President [[Bill Clinton]] to serve on the [[United States Arctic Research Commission|Arctic Research Commission]] in order to develop and recommend an integrated national policy on research in the Arctic.<ref>{{cite web |title=President Picks UT Oceanographer |url=https://news.utk.edu/2000/03/13/president-picks-ut-oceanographer/ |publisher=University of Tennessee |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=March 13, 2000}}</ref> Following this, she served as part of a team studying the relationship between plankton in the ocean surrounding Antarctica and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite web |title=Antarctic Plankton Reduces Greenhouse Gases |url=https://news.utk.edu/2000/04/10/antarctic-plankton-reduces-greenhouse-gases/ |publisher=University of Tennessee |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=April 10, 2000}}</ref> In 2006, Grebmeier and her colleagues published the seminal paper, "A major ecosystem shift in the northern Bering Sea" in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'',<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grebmeier |first1=Jacqueline M. |last2=Overland |first2=James E. |last3=Moore |first3=Sue E. |last4=Farley |first4=Ed V. |last5=Carmack |first5=Eddy C. |last6=Cooper |first6=Lee W. |last7=Frey |first7=Karen E. |last8=Helle |first8=John H. |last9=McLaughlin |first9=Fiona A. |last10=McNutt |first10=S. Lyn |title=A Major Ecosystem Shift in the Northern Bering Sea |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |date=March 10, 2006 |volume=311 |issue=5766 |pages=1461–1464 |doi=10.1126/science.1121365 |pmid=16527980 |bibcode=2006Sci...311.1461G |s2cid=23505224 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1121365 |access-date=January 6, 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which showed the harms of global warming in the ecology of the Bering Sea.<ref>{{cite web |title=UT Research Shows Ecological Impact of Global Warming |url=https://news.utk.edu/2006/03/09/ut-research-shows-ecological-impact-of-global-warming/ |publisher=University of Tennessee |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=March 9, 2006}}</ref>

Grebmeier was appointed a research professor at the [[University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science]], working in the [[Chesapeake Biological Laboratory]], in 2008.<ref name="bio">{{cite web |title=Jacqueline M. Grebmeier |url=https://arctic.cbl.umces.edu/web-content/Jacqueline_Grebmeier/index.html |website=umces.edu |access-date=June 6, 2021}}</ref> While serving in this role, she chaired the International Pacific Arctic Group to establish a Distributed Biological Observatory in the North American Arctic.<ref>{{cite web |title=BIOLOGISTS LEAD INTERNATIONAL TEAM TO TRACK ARCTIC RESPONSE TO CLIMATE CHANGE |work=University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science |url=https://www.umces.edu/cbl/mdsg/story/2013/feb/20/biologists-lead-international-team-track-arctic-response-climate-change |publisher=University of Maryland |access-date=June 6, 2020 |date=February 20, 2013 |archive-date=September 18, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918235607/https://www.umces.edu/cbl/mdsg/story/2013/feb/20/biologists-lead-international-team-track-arctic-response-climate-change |url-status=dead }}</ref> As a result of her "exceptional and sustained contributions to the understanding of the Arctic" Grebmeier was awarded the 2015 IASC Medal<ref>{{cite web |title=DR. JACQUELINE GREBMEIER AWARDED IASC MEDAL |url=https://www.umces.edu/cbl/story/2015/mar/09/dr-jacqueline-grebmeier-awarded-iasc-medal |publisher=University of Maryland |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=March 9, 2015}}</ref> and the Alaska Ocean Leadership Award from the Alaska SeaLife Center.<ref>{{cite web |title=ARCTIC SCIENTISTS RECEIVE MARINE RESEARCH AWARD |url=https://www.umces.edu/cbl/story/2015/jan/30/arctic-scientists-receive-marine-research-award |publisher=University of Maryland |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=January 30, 2015}}</ref> The following year, she won the 2016 President's Award for Excellence in Application of Science for her "exceptional and sustained contributions to the understanding of the Arctic."<ref>{{cite web |title=DR. JACQUELINE GREBMEIER HONORED WITH PRESIDENT'S AWARD FOR SCIENCE APPLICATION |url=https://www.umces.edu/cbl/release/2016/may/18/dr-jacqueline-grebmeier-honored-president%E2%80%99s-award-science-application |publisher=University of Maryland |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=May 18, 2016}}</ref>

In 2018, Grebmeier was elected a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{cite web |title=ARCTIC RESEARCHER JACQUELINE GREBMEIER NAMED AAAS FELLOW |url=https://www.umces.edu/news/arctic-researcher-jacqueline-grebmeier-named-aaas-fellow |publisher=University of Maryland |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=November 27, 2018}}</ref> During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], Grebmeier raised the alarm on the rising disappearing Alaskan sea ice and its significant impact on the Arctic marine ecosystem.<ref>{{cite web |title=Disappearing Alaskan sea ice is significant for Arctic marine ecosystem |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2020/04/200422151134.htm |publisher=Science Daily |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=April 22, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Grebmeier is married to Lee Cooper, an oceanographer,<ref>{{cite web |title=Arctic Life Not Damaged By Nuclear Waste Dumping (400) |url=https://news.utk.edu/1998/06/09/arctic-life-not-damaged-by-nuclear-waste-dumping-400/ |publisher=University of Tennessee |access-date=June 6, 2021 |date=June 9, 1998}}</ref> and they have one daughter together.<ref name="Holden">{{cite news |last1=Holden |first1=Emily |title='We packed long underwear and never wore it': Arctic scientists shocked at warming |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/nov/13/arctic-melting-climate-change |access-date=June 6, 2021 |work=The Guardian |date=November 13, 2020}}</ref>
